code: print(sum((50 * 10**8 >> era) * 210000 for era in range(33)) / 10**8)
why: The sum of every era's subsidy falls just short of 21 million because each era's subsidy is rounded down to whole satoshi.
Shifting 50 * 10**8 satoshi right by four places halves it four times, which leaves 3.125 bitcoin.

code:
import hashlib
n = 0
while not hashlib.sha256(f'SEN0401-{n}'.encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0000'):
    n += 1
print(n)
why: The loop counts nonces until the SHA-256 hash of SEN0401 and the nonce starts with four zeros; the first such nonce is 15083.

q: Why is proof of work useful for agreeing on a block?
options: It is costly to produce but cheap for anyone to verify
It encrypts the block so that only miners can read it
It lets one trusted server decide which block is valid
It makes every block exactly the same size
why: Finding the nonce takes many hash attempts, while checking it takes a single hash, so everyone can confirm that the work was done.

q: In the book's convention, what does the capital letter in Bitcoin mark?
options: The unit of currency, as opposed to the network
The system, as opposed to the unit called bitcoin
The largest denomination of the currency
The first version of the software
why: The unit of currency is bitcoin with a small b and the system is Bitcoin with a capital B.

options: The wallet stores no addresses at all
A bank holds the keys for the user
Only the user holds the keys that control the bitcoin
The wallet runs only on a desktop computer
why: Whoever controls the private keys controls the bitcoin, and in a noncustodial wallet that is the user alone.

options: Paying a transaction fee twice for one transfer
Two miners finding the same block at once
Receiving the same address from two wallets
Spending the same unit of digital money twice
why: A digital token can be copied, so a system without a central clearinghouse needs a rule that stops the same unit being spent twice.
